## Search method v007

Define X and Y exactly, including entity unit, exclusions, effective dates, eligible subtypes and group-membership rules. Start sequentially with one X-only search, one Y-only search and one conjunction search, using the user's broad predicate wording rather than a familiar subtype. Maintain deduplicated X/Y frontiers and an identity/evidence ledger. Also maintain a compact scope ledger: for each discovery query record added restrictions not required by the hunt (subtype, occupation, geography, era, source or familiar-name terms). A successful restricted query does not establish coverage of its parent category. Derive a few meaningful sibling partitions from source taxonomies or the eligibility definition; do not invent an exhaustive cross-product or enumerate a whole census by default. Run short discovery/check rounds, prioritizing expected verified additions per total resolution cost. Each round's neglected-subtype or reverse-frontier probe must address a specific untested scope-ledger cell or remove a recorded accidental restriction; merely paraphrasing a prior conjunction does not qualify. Check source-backed candidates on Parallel for only unresolved predicates, supplying identity and existing evidence. Use small affordable batches, price every candidate, and do not recheck established facts. No result means unresolved, not false; reject only on contradiction or an exhaustive applicable source. Escalate promising ambiguous or conflicting cases individually to Exa. After two discovery searches add no plausible identities, prohibit synonymous conjunction searches and perform a residual-scope pass: identify the most consequential restriction accumulated so far, try a sibling subtype or unrestricted parent on the opposite frontier, then resolve resulting candidates before further discovery. Reserve at least 35% of initial funds for evidence and stop discovery whenever pending checks require the remaining funds. Before submitting with spare funds, perform up to three affordable residual probes covering distinct untested restrictions or source partitions, retaining enough funds to verify their likely candidates. Stop this pass after two probes add neither candidates nor useful evidence; do not spend merely to exhaust the budget. Finish with identity, predicate, subtype and effective-date audits; submit supported intersections only and never infer completeness from saturation.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['parallel'].

Price candidate batches as the sum of queries and provider charges; fewer results are not presumed cheaper. Exa alone with 4 results for selected unresolved identities where ambiguity, conflicting evidence or inaccessibility warrants the higher cost. At most one initial Exa discovery probe after Parallel stagnation, continued only if it contributes useful new identities or evidence. Try a genuinely different scope partition on Parallel before buying provider diversity for a repetitive query. Authoritative-domain filters are for targeted evidence, not general frontier coverage; relax failed filters. Use publication-date filters only when publication date itself determines eligibility, and verify effective dates in content.

### Fetch policy
Reuse cached source facts. Fetch authoritative pages that can settle missing identity or predicates, and useful multi-candidate lists, rather than every result. When a list is used for scope coverage, inspect its stated subtype, date range and pagination/section links; an excerpt or one section is not an exhausted category. Follow only sections tied to a promising uncovered partition, without committing to bulk census extraction. After a blocked or uninformative page, make one targeted alternate-source attempt rather than a fetch chain.

## SiftText

At the start of every new chat, unless I say not to use SiftText, before any other tool call:
1. Run `sifttext instructions`.
2. Read the Entry above and follow it, plus any `agent-instructions` the command returns.
3. Before retrieving knowledge, read the Retrieval guide above, do not search first.

## Tooling policy

- Never directly invoke `python`, `python3`, `pip`, or `pip3` unless explicitly instructed by the human.
- Use `uv` for all agent-initiated Python work:
  - Python execution: `uv run python ...`
  - Scripts and tests: `uv run ...`
  - Throwaway dependencies: `uv run --with <package> ...`
  - Python CLI tools: `uvx <tool>`
  - Durable project dependencies: use the project's appropriate `uv` command and preserve its lockfile.
- For non-Python probing or testing with unavailable tools:
  - One executable: `nix run nixpkgs#<package> -- <args>`
  - Temporary environment: `nix shell nixpkgs#<package> ... --command <command>`
- Nix environments are temporary, but downloaded store paths may remain cached until garbage collection.
- If a Nix dependency becomes useful for recurring or future work, tell the human and suggest adding it to the appropriate durable Nix configuration (such as a project flake/dev shell, Home Manager, or nix-darwin configuration). Do not make that durable change unless asked.

</addendum>

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

### Mercury Craters Named for Authors & Poets

\![MESSENGER](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/blogger_img_proxy/AEn0k_v4rp-kJn7UTGXlsOZppzZXpJKzhrvA4sIdOoHUuy-6q0Sa8abxAPXRTJSId7NFwgW8Ulj_-PhibEEf8D-xzGczhtp1EGIk9TxE6_gHdXjLSHqmGZ3b=s0-d)  
   
 *Image of the Planet Mercury.*  
 *(Image Source: [http://messenger.jhuapl.edu](http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/) )*  
   
 **MESSENGER Mission News**  
 March 26, 2013   
   
 The International Astronomical Union (IAU) — the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919 — recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign names to nine impact craters on Mercury. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors or other contributors to the humanities.  
   
 The newly named craters include for the following authors and poets:  
   
 **L'Engle**, for Madeleine L'Engle (1918-2007), an American writer best known for young-adult fiction, particularly the award-winning *A Wrinkle in Time* and its sequels: *A Wind in the Door*, *A Swiftly Tilting Planet*, *Many Waters*, and *An Acceptable Time*. Her works reflect both her Christian faith and her strong interest in modern science.  
   
 **Alver**, for Betti Alver (1906-1989), an Estonian writer who rose to prominence in the 1930s, toward the end of Estonian independence and on the eve of World War II. She published her first novel, *Mistress in the Wind*, in 1927. She also wrote several short stories, poetry, and translations.  
   
 **Donelaitis**, for Kristijonas Donelaitis (1714-1780), a Lutheran pastor who was considered one of the greatest Lithuanian poets. He is best known for *The Seasons*, considered the first classic Lithuanian poem. It depicts the everyday life of Lithuanian peasants. His other works include six fables and a tale in verse.  
   
 **Flaiano**, for Ennio Flaiano (1910-1972), an Italian screenwriter, playwright, novelist, journalist, and drama critic especially noted for his social satires. He became a leading figure of the Italian motion-picture industry after World War II, collaborating with writer Tullio Pinelli on the early films of writer and director Federico Fellini.  
   
 **Lovecraft**, for Howard Phillips Lovecraft (1890-1937), an American author of horror, fantasy, and science fiction regarded as one of the most influential horror writers of the 20th Century. He popularized "cosmic horror," the notion that some concepts, entities, or experiences are barely comprehensible to human minds, and those who delve into such topics risk their sanity.  
   
 **Petofi**, for Sandor Petofi (1823-1849), a Hungarian poet and liberal revolutionary. He wrote the *Nemzeti dal* (National Poem), which is said to have inspired the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 that grew into a war for independence from the Austrian Empire.

### Mercury Craters Named for Authors & Poets

\![MESSENGER](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/blogger_img_proxy/AEn0k_v4rp-kJn7UTGXlsOZppzZXpJKzhrvA4sIdOoHUuy-6q0Sa8abxAPXRTJSId7NFwgW8Ulj_-PhibEEf8D-xzGczhtp1EGIk9TxE6_gHdXjLSHqmGZ3b=s0-d)  
   
 *Image of the Planet Mercury.*  
 *(Image Source: [http://messenger.jhuapl.edu](http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/) )*  
   
 **MESSENGER Mission News**  
 March 26, 2013   
   
 The International Astronomical Union (IAU) — the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919 — recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign names to nine impact craters on Mercury. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors or other contributors to the humanities.  
   
 The newly named craters include for the following authors and poets:  
   
 **L'Engle**, for Madeleine L'Engle (1918-2007), an American writer best known for young-adult fiction, particularly the award-winning *A Wrinkle in Time* and its sequels: *A Wind in the Door*, *A Swiftly Tilting Planet*, *Many Waters*, and *An Acceptable Time*. Her works reflect both her Christian faith and her strong interest in modern science.  
   
 **Alver**, for Betti Alver (1906-1989), an Estonian writer who rose to prominence in the 1930s, toward the end of Estonian independence and on the eve of World War II. She published her first novel, *Mistress in the Wind*, in 1927. She also wrote several short stories, poetry, and translations.  
   
 **Donelaitis**, for Kristijonas Donelaitis (1714-1780), a Lutheran pastor who was considered one of the greatest Lithuanian poets. He is best known for *The Seasons*, considered the first classic Lithuanian poem. It depicts the everyday life of Lithuanian peasants. His other works include six fables and a tale in verse.  
   
 **Flaiano**, for Ennio Flaiano (1910-1972), an Italian screenwriter, playwright, novelist, journalist, and drama critic especially noted for his social satires. He became a leading figure of the Italian motion-picture industry after World War II, collaborating with writer Tullio Pinelli on the early films of writer and director Federico Fellini.  
   
 **Lovecraft**, for Howard Phillips Lovecraft (1890-1937), an American author of horror, fantasy, and science fiction regarded as one of the most influential horror writers of the 20th Century. He popularized "cosmic horror," the notion that some concepts, entities, or experiences are barely comprehensible to human minds, and those who delve into such topics risk their sanity.  
   
 **Petofi**, for Sandor Petofi (1823-1849), a Hungarian poet and liberal revolutionary. He wrote the *Nemzeti dal* (National Poem), which is said to have inspired the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 that grew into a war for independence from the Austrian Empire.

### Mercury Craters Named for Authors & Poets

\![MESSENGER](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/blogger_img_proxy/AEn0k_v4rp-kJn7UTGXlsOZppzZXpJKzhrvA4sIdOoHUuy-6q0Sa8abxAPXRTJSId7NFwgW8Ulj_-PhibEEf8D-xzGczhtp1EGIk9TxE6_gHdXjLSHqmGZ3b=s0-d)  
   
 *Image of the Planet Mercury.*  
 *(Image Source: [http://messenger.jhuapl.edu](http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/) )*  
   
 **MESSENGER Mission News**  
 March 26, 2013   
   
 The International Astronomical Union (IAU) — the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919 — recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign names to nine impact craters on Mercury. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors or other contributors to the humanities.  
   
 The newly named craters include for the following authors and poets:  
   
 **L'Engle**, for Madeleine L'Engle (1918-2007), an American writer best known for young-adult fiction, particularly the award-winning *A Wrinkle in Time* and its sequels: *A Wind in the Door*, *A Swiftly Tilting Planet*, *Many Waters*, and *An Acceptable Time*. Her works reflect both her Christian faith and her strong interest in modern science.  
   
 **Alver**, for Betti Alver (1906-1989), an Estonian writer who rose to prominence in the 1930s, toward the end of Estonian independence and on the eve of World War II. She published her first novel, *Mistress in the Wind*, in 1927. She also wrote several short stories, poetry, and translations.  
   
 **Donelaitis**, for Kristijonas Donelaitis (1714-1780), a Lutheran pastor who was considered one of the greatest Lithuanian poets. He is best known for *The Seasons*, considered the first classic Lithuanian poem. It depicts the everyday life of Lithuanian peasants. His other works include six fables and a tale in verse.  
   
 **Flaiano**, for Ennio Flaiano (1910-1972), an Italian screenwriter, playwright, novelist, journalist, and drama critic especially noted for his social satires. He became a leading figure of the Italian motion-picture industry after World War II, collaborating with writer Tullio Pinelli on the early films of writer and director Federico Fellini.  
   
 **Lovecraft**, for Howard Phillips Lovecraft (1890-1937), an American author of horror, fantasy, and science fiction regarded as one of the most influential horror writers of the 20th Century. He popularized "cosmic horror," the notion that some concepts, entities, or experiences are barely comprehensible to human minds, and those who delve into such topics risk their sanity.  
   
 **Petofi**, for Sandor Petofi (1823-1849), a Hungarian poet and liberal revolutionary. He wrote the *Nemzeti dal* (National Poem), which is said to have inspired the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 that grew into a war for independence from the Austrian Empire.

### Mercury Craters Named for Authors & Poets

\![MESSENGER](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/blogger_img_proxy/AEn0k_v4rp-kJn7UTGXlsOZppzZXpJKzhrvA4sIdOoHUuy-6q0Sa8abxAPXRTJSId7NFwgW8Ulj_-PhibEEf8D-xzGczhtp1EGIk9TxE6_gHdXjLSHqmGZ3b=s0-d)  
   
 *Image of the Planet Mercury.*  
 *(Image Source: [http://messenger.jhuapl.edu](http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/) )*  
   
 **MESSENGER Mission News**  
 March 26, 2013   
   
 The International Astronomical Union (IAU) — the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919 — recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign names to nine impact craters on Mercury. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors or other contributors to the humanities.  
   
 The newly named craters include for the following authors and poets:  
   
 **L'Engle**, for Madeleine L'Engle (1918-2007), an American writer best known for young-adult fiction, particularly the award-winning *A Wrinkle in Time* and its sequels: *A Wind in the Door*, *A Swiftly Tilting Planet*, *Many Waters*, and *An Acceptable Time*. Her works reflect both her Christian faith and her strong interest in modern science.  
   
 **Alver**, for Betti Alver (1906-1989), an Estonian writer who rose to prominence in the 1930s, toward the end of Estonian independence and on the eve of World War II. She published her first novel, *Mistress in the Wind*, in 1927. She also wrote several short stories, poetry, and translations.  
   
 **Donelaitis**, for Kristijonas Donelaitis (1714-1780), a Lutheran pastor who was considered one of the greatest Lithuanian poets. He is best known for *The Seasons*, considered the first classic Lithuanian poem. It depicts the everyday life of Lithuanian peasants. His other works include six fables and a tale in verse.  
   
 **Flaiano**, for Ennio Flaiano (1910-1972), an Italian screenwriter, playwright, novelist, journalist, and drama critic especially noted for his social satires. He became a leading figure of the Italian motion-picture industry after World War II, collaborating with writer Tullio Pinelli on the early films of writer and director Federico Fellini.  
   
 **Lovecraft**, for Howard Phillips Lovecraft (1890-1937), an American author of horror, fantasy, and science fiction regarded as one of the most influential horror writers of the 20th Century. He popularized "cosmic horror," the notion that some concepts, entities, or experiences are barely comprehensible to human minds, and those who delve into such topics risk their sanity.  
   
 **Petofi**, for Sandor Petofi (1823-1849), a Hungarian poet and liberal revolutionary. He wrote the *Nemzeti dal* (National Poem), which is said to have inspired the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 that grew into a war for independence from the Austrian Empire.

Mercury

The planet Mercury has just under 400 craters. The wonderful part is that most of them are named for famous people in the arts: writers, artists and composers. The rule for inclusion is that “all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.”

*Haydn: Symphony No. 43 in E-Flat Major, Hob.I:43, “Mercury” – IV. Allegro (Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment; Frans Brüggen, cond.)*

In looking over the list, we find some 50 craters named after composers, conductors, and musicians. [Gluck](https://interlude.hk/skipping-town-christoph-willibald-gluck/) and [Debussy](https://interlude.hk/claude-achille-debussy/) rub shoulders with John Lennon and Machaut. They come from countries all over the world, from India to Italy, Austria to America, and China to Brazil. They are predominantly male, but [Alicia de Larrocha](https://interlude.hk/great-women-artists-shaped-music-v-alicia-de-larrocha/) (Spain) does sweep in as does Cai Wenji (China) and Umm Kulthum (Egypt).

*Strauss I: Merkurs Flugel, Walzer (Wings of Mercury, Waltz), Op. 83 (Slovak Sinfonietta, Žilina; Christian Pollack, cond.)*

When you look at the map of Mercury recently developed by the US Geological Survey, we can find out where our composers are.

Sometimes the juxtapositions of names seem a bit random and other times, done with a clever sense of humour: Berlioz next to Carolan (top left), Purcell next to the painter van Dijck/Dyck (center top), and right in the middle of the planet is Mozart. Debussy is by Joplin (bottom left) and above Lennon, is Holst.

## [Julie K. Brown](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/julie-k-brown)

A special citation is awarded to Miami Herald reporter Julie K. Brown for her groundbreaking reporting in 2017 and 2018 that exposed Jeffrey Epstein’s systematic abuse of young women, the justice system that protected him, and, over time, his powerful network of associates and enablers. Her Perversion of Justice series, published nearly a decade ago, revealed how prosecutors shielded Epstein from federal sex trafficking charges when he was first accused of abusing young women. She went on to document and give voice to the scores of victims who had been groomed and abused by him and others in his circle. Her work, and the release of the government’s Epstein files, continue to reverberate around the world.

## [Greg Tate](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/greg-tate)

A special citation for the late writer and critic Greg Tate, whose language – cribbed from literature, academia, popular culture and hip-hop – was as influential as the content of his ideas. His aesthetic, innovations and intellectual originality, particularly in his pioneering hip-hop criticism, continue to influence subsequent generations, especially writers and critics of color.


## [Journalists and Media Workers Covering the War in Gaza](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/journalists-and-media-workers-covering-war-gaza)

In recent years the Pulitzer Board has issued citations honoring journalists covering wars in Ukraine and Afghanistan. This year, the Board recognizes the courageous work of journalists and media workers covering the war in Gaza. Under horrific conditions, an extraordinary number of journalists have died in the effort to tell the stories of Palestinians and others in Gaza. This war has also claimed the lives of poets and writers among the casualties. As the Pulitzer Prizes honor categories of journalism, arts, and letters, we mark the loss of invaluable records of the human experience.

## [The Journalists of Ukraine](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/journalists-ukraine)

The Pulitzer Board awards a special citation to the journalists of Ukraine for their courage, endurance, and commitment to truthful reporting during Vladimir Putin’s ruthless invasion of their country and his propaganda war in Russia. Despite bombardment, abductions, occupation, and even deaths in their ranks, they have persisted in their effort to provide an accurate picture of a terrible reality, doing honor to Ukraine and to journalists around the world.

## [Afghanistan Journalism Workers](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/afghanistan-journalism-workers)

A special citation to honor the women and men of Afghanistan who have dedicated themselves at great personal risk to create and support journalism that has chronicled decades of life and war. From staff and freelance correspondents to interpreters to drivers to hosts, courageous Afghan residents helped produce Pulitzer-winning and Pulitzer-worthy images and stories that have contributed to a wider understanding of profoundly tragic and complicated circumstances. In support of their safety in either their continued work or their resettlement, this citation comes with a $100,000 grant to be administered by the Committee to Protect Journalists for the emergency relief of such individuals and their families. Mercury

The planet Mercury has just under 400 craters. The wonderful part is that most of them are named for famous people in the arts: writers, artists and composers. The rule for inclusion is that “all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.”

*Haydn: Symphony No. 43 in E-Flat Major, Hob.I:43, “Mercury” – IV. Allegro (Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment; Frans Brüggen, cond.)*

In looking over the list, we find some 50 craters named after composers, conductors, and musicians. [Gluck](https://interlude.hk/skipping-town-christoph-willibald-gluck/) and [Debussy](https://interlude.hk/claude-achille-debussy/) rub shoulders with John Lennon and Machaut. They come from countries all over the world, from India to Italy, Austria to America, and China to Brazil. They are predominantly male, but [Alicia de Larrocha](https://interlude.hk/great-women-artists-shaped-music-v-alicia-de-larrocha/) (Spain) does sweep in as does Cai Wenji (China) and Umm Kulthum (Egypt).

*Strauss I: Merkurs Flugel, Walzer (Wings of Mercury, Waltz), Op. 83 (Slovak Sinfonietta, Žilina; Christian Pollack, cond.)*

*Holst: The Planets: III. Mercury, The Winged Messenger (Royal Scottish National Orchestra; David Lloyd-Jones, cond.)*

When you look at the map of Mercury recently developed by the US Geological Survey, we can find out where our composers are.

Sometimes the juxtapositions of names seem a bit random and other times, done with a clever sense of humour: Berlioz next to Carolan (top left), Purcell next to the painter van Dijck/Dyck (center top), and right in the middle of the planet is Mozart. Debussy is by Joplin (bottom left) and above Lennon, is Holst.

Mercury

The planet Mercury has just under 400 craters. The wonderful part is that most of them are named for famous people in the arts: writers, artists and composers. The rule for inclusion is that “all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.”

*Haydn: Symphony No. 43 in E-Flat Major, Hob.I:43, “Mercury” – IV. Allegro (Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment; Frans Brüggen, cond.)*

In looking over the list, we find some 50 craters named after composers, conductors, and musicians. [Gluck](https://interlude.hk/skipping-town-christoph-willibald-gluck/) and [Debussy](https://interlude.hk/claude-achille-debussy/) rub shoulders with John Lennon and Machaut. They come from countries all over the world, from India to Italy, Austria to America, and China to Brazil. They are predominantly male, but [Alicia de Larrocha](https://interlude.hk/great-women-artists-shaped-music-v-alicia-de-larrocha/) (Spain) does sweep in as does Cai Wenji (China) and Umm Kulthum (Egypt).

*Strauss I: Merkurs Flugel, Walzer (Wings of Mercury, Waltz), Op. 83 (Slovak Sinfonietta, Žilina; Christian Pollack, cond.)*

*Holst: The Planets: III. Mercury, The Winged Messenger (Royal Scottish National Orchestra; David Lloyd-Jones, cond.)*

When you look at the map of Mercury recently developed by the US Geological Survey, we can find out where our composers are.

Sometimes the juxtapositions of names seem a bit random and other times, done with a clever sense of humour: Berlioz next to Carolan (top left), Purcell next to the painter van Dijck/Dyck (center top), and right in the middle of the planet is Mozart. Debussy is by Joplin (bottom left) and above Lennon, is Holst.

Mercury

The planet Mercury has just under 400 craters. The wonderful part is that most of them are named for famous people in the arts: writers, artists and composers. The rule for inclusion is that “all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.”

*Haydn: Symphony No. 43 in E-Flat Major, Hob.I:43, “Mercury” – IV. Allegro (Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment; Frans Brüggen, cond.)*

In looking over the list, we find some 50 craters named after composers, conductors, and musicians. [Gluck](https://interlude.hk/skipping-town-christoph-willibald-gluck/) and [Debussy](https://interlude.hk/claude-achille-debussy/) rub shoulders with John Lennon and Machaut. They come from countries all over the world, from India to Italy, Austria to America, and China to Brazil. They are predominantly male, but [Alicia de Larrocha](https://interlude.hk/great-women-artists-shaped-music-v-alicia-de-larrocha/) (Spain) does sweep in as does Cai Wenji (China) and Umm Kulthum (Egypt).

*Strauss I: Merkurs Flugel, Walzer (Wings of Mercury, Waltz), Op. 83 (Slovak Sinfonietta, Žilina; Christian Pollack, cond.)*

*Holst: The Planets: III. Mercury, The Winged Messenger (Royal Scottish National Orchestra; David Lloyd-Jones, cond.)*

When you look at the map of Mercury recently developed by the US Geological Survey, we can find out where our composers are.

Sometimes the juxtapositions of names seem a bit random and other times, done with a clever sense of humour: Berlioz next to Carolan (top left), Purcell next to the painter van Dijck/Dyck (center top), and right in the middle of the planet is Mozart. Debussy is by Joplin (bottom left) and above Lennon, is Holst.

You are a web search agent. Follow your search method.

## Search method v007

Define X and Y exactly, including entity unit, exclusions, effective dates, eligible subtypes and group-membership rules. Start sequentially with one X-only search, one Y-only search and one conjunction search, using the user's broad predicate wording rather than a familiar subtype. Maintain deduplicated X/Y frontiers and an identity/evidence ledger. Also maintain a compact scope ledger: for each discovery query record added restrictions not required by the hunt (subtype, occupation, geography, era, source or familiar-name terms). A successful restricted query does not establish coverage of its parent category. Derive a few meaningful sibling partitions from source taxonomies or the eligibility definition; do not invent an exhaustive cross-product or enumerate a whole census by default. Run short discovery/check rounds, prioritizing expected verified additions per total resolution cost. Each round's neglected-subtype or reverse-frontier probe must address a specific untested scope-ledger cell or remove a recorded accidental restriction; merely paraphrasing a prior conjunction does not qualify. Check source-backed candidates on Parallel for only unresolved predicates, supplying identity and existing evidence. Use small affordable batches, price every candidate, and do not recheck established facts. No result means unresolved, not false; reject only on contradiction or an exhaustive applicable source. Escalate promising ambiguous or conflicting cases individually to Exa. After two discovery searches add no plausible identities, prohibit synonymous conjunction searches and perform a residual-scope pass: identify the most consequential restriction accumulated so far, try a sibling subtype or unrestricted parent on the opposite frontier, then resolve resulting candidates before further discovery. Reserve at least 35% of initial funds for evidence and stop discovery whenever pending checks require the remaining funds. Before submitting with spare funds, perform up to three affordable residual probes covering distinct untested restrictions or source partitions, retaining enough funds to verify their likely candidates. Stop this pass after two probes add neither candidates nor useful evidence; do not spend merely to exhaust the budget. Finish with identity, predicate, subtype and effective-date audits; submit supported intersections only and never infer completeness from saturation.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['parallel'].
Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results for baseline and residual discovery, 4 for exact missing-fact checks. No routine also variants or broad auto-routing. Price candidate batches as the sum of queries and provider charges; fewer results are not presumed cheaper. Exa alone with 4 results for selected unresolved identities where ambiguity, conflicting evidence or inaccessibility warrants the higher cost. At most one initial Exa discovery probe after Parallel stagnation, continued only if it contributes useful new identities or evidence. Try a genuinely different scope partition on Parallel before buying provider diversity for a repetitive query. Authoritative-domain filters are for targeted evidence, not general frontier coverage; relax failed filters. Use publication-date filters only when publication date itself determines eligibility, and verify effective dates in content.

### Fetch policy
Reuse cached source facts. Fetch authoritative pages that can settle missing identity or predicates, and useful multi-candidate lists, rather than every result. When a list is used for scope coverage, inspect its stated subtype, date range and pagination/section links; an excerpt or one section is not an exhausted category. Follow only sections tied to a promising uncovered partition, without committing to bulk census extraction. After a blocked or uninformative page, make one targeted alternate-source attempt rather than a fetch chain.

Appearance

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

### Mercury Craters Named for Authors & Poets

\![MESSENGER](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/blogger_img_proxy/AEn0k_v4rp-kJn7UTGXlsOZppzZXpJKzhrvA4sIdOoHUuy-6q0Sa8abxAPXRTJSId7NFwgW8Ulj_-PhibEEf8D-xzGczhtp1EGIk9TxE6_gHdXjLSHqmGZ3b=s0-d)  
   
 *Image of the Planet Mercury.*  
 *(Image Source: [http://messenger.jhuapl.edu](http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/) )*  
   
 **MESSENGER Mission News**  
 March 26, 2013   
   
 The International Astronomical Union (IAU) — the arbiter of planetary and satellite nomenclature since its inception in 1919 — recently approved a proposal from the MESSENGER Science Team to assign names to nine impact craters on Mercury. In keeping with the established naming theme for craters on Mercury, all of the newly designated features are named after famous deceased artists, musicians, or authors or other contributors to the humanities.  
   
 The newly named craters include for the following authors and poets:  
   
 **L'Engle**, for Madeleine L'Engle (1918-2007), an American writer best known for young-adult fiction, particularly the award-winning *A Wrinkle in Time* and its sequels: *A Wind in the Door*, *A Swiftly Tilting Planet*, *Many Waters*, and *An Acceptable Time*. Her works reflect both her Christian faith and her strong interest in modern science.  
   
 **Alver**, for Betti Alver (1906-1989), an Estonian writer who rose to prominence in the 1930s, toward the end of Estonian independence and on the eve of World War II. She published her first novel, *Mistress in the Wind*, in 1927. She also wrote several short stories, poetry, and translations.  
   
 **Donelaitis**, for Kristijonas Donelaitis (1714-1780), a Lutheran pastor who was considered one of the greatest Lithuanian poets. He is best known for *The Seasons*, considered the first classic Lithuanian poem. It depicts the everyday life of Lithuanian peasants. His other works include six fables and a tale in verse.  
   
 **Flaiano**, for Ennio Flaiano (1910-1972), an Italian screenwriter, playwright, novelist, journalist, and drama critic especially noted for his social satires. He became a leading figure of the Italian motion-picture industry after World War II, collaborating with writer Tullio Pinelli on the early films of writer and director Federico Fellini.  
   
 **Lovecraft**, for Howard Phillips Lovecraft (1890-1937), an American author of horror, fantasy, and science fiction regarded as one of the most influential horror writers of the 20th Century. He popularized "cosmic horror," the notion that some concepts, entities, or experiences are barely comprehensible to human minds, and those who delve into such topics risk their sanity.  
   
 **Petofi**, for Sandor Petofi (1823-1849), a Hungarian poet and liberal revolutionary. He wrote the *Nemzeti dal* (National Poem), which is said to have inspired the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 that grew into a war for independence from the Austrian Empire.

Mercury

The planet Mercury has just under 400 craters. The wonderful part is that most of them are named for famous people in the arts: writers, artists and composers. The rule for inclusion is that “all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.”

*Haydn: Symphony No. 43 in E-Flat Major, Hob.I:43, “Mercury” – IV. Allegro (Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment; Frans Brüggen, cond.)*

In looking over the list, we find some 50 craters named after composers, conductors, and musicians. [Gluck](https://interlude.hk/skipping-town-christoph-willibald-gluck/) and [Debussy](https://interlude.hk/claude-achille-debussy/) rub shoulders with John Lennon and Machaut. They come from countries all over the world, from India to Italy, Austria to America, and China to Brazil. They are predominantly male, but [Alicia de Larrocha](https://interlude.hk/great-women-artists-shaped-music-v-alicia-de-larrocha/) (Spain) does sweep in as does Cai Wenji (China) and Umm Kulthum (Egypt).

*Strauss I: Merkurs Flugel, Walzer (Wings of Mercury, Waltz), Op. 83 (Slovak Sinfonietta, Žilina; Christian Pollack, cond.)*

When you look at the map of Mercury recently developed by the US Geological Survey, we can find out where our composers are.

Sometimes the juxtapositions of names seem a bit random and other times, done with a clever sense of humour: Berlioz next to Carolan (top left), Purcell next to the painter van Dijck/Dyck (center top), and right in the middle of the planet is Mozart. Debussy is by Joplin (bottom left) and above Lennon, is Holst.

## [Julie K. Brown](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/julie-k-brown)

A special citation is awarded to Miami Herald reporter Julie K. Brown for her groundbreaking reporting in 2017 and 2018 that exposed Jeffrey Epstein’s systematic abuse of young women, the justice system that protected him, and, over time, his powerful network of associates and enablers. Her Perversion of Justice series, published nearly a decade ago, revealed how prosecutors shielded Epstein from federal sex trafficking charges when he was first accused of abusing young women. She went on to document and give voice to the scores of victims who had been groomed and abused by him and others in his circle. Her work, and the release of the government’s Epstein files, continue to reverberate around the world.

## [Greg Tate](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/greg-tate)

A special citation for the late writer and critic Greg Tate, whose language – cribbed from literature, academia, popular culture and hip-hop – was as influential as the content of his ideas. His aesthetic, innovations and intellectual originality, particularly in his pioneering hip-hop criticism, continue to influence subsequent generations, especially writers and critics of color.


## [Journalists and Media Workers Covering the War in Gaza](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/journalists-and-media-workers-covering-war-gaza)

In recent years the Pulitzer Board has issued citations honoring journalists covering wars in Ukraine and Afghanistan. This year, the Board recognizes the courageous work of journalists and media workers covering the war in Gaza. Under horrific conditions, an extraordinary number of journalists have died in the effort to tell the stories of Palestinians and others in Gaza. This war has also claimed the lives of poets and writers among the casualties. As the Pulitzer Prizes honor categories of journalism, arts, and letters, we mark the loss of invaluable records of the human experience.

The Pulitzer Board awards a special citation to the journalists of Ukraine for their courage, endurance, and commitment to truthful reporting during Vladimir Putin’s ruthless invasion of their country and his propaganda war in Russia. Despite bombardment, abductions, occupation, and even deaths in their ranks, they have persisted in their effort to provide an accurate picture of a terrible reality, doing honor to Ukraine and to journalists around the world.

## [Afghanistan Journalism Workers](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/afghanistan-journalism-workers)

A special citation to honor the women and men of Afghanistan who have dedicated themselves at great personal risk to create and support journalism that has chronicled decades of life and war. From staff and freelance correspondents to interpreters to drivers to hosts, courageous Afghan residents helped produce Pulitzer-winning and Pulitzer-worthy images and stories that have contributed to a wider understanding of profoundly tragic and complicated circumstances.
